extracted.intended_audience: individuals applying for registration to practice patent matters before the USPTO; OED examiners, counsel, and regulators
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria the USPTO (OED Director and Director) applies when determining whether an individual possesses the good moral character and reputation required for registration to practice patent matters before the Office, including disclosure duties, candor, misconduct assessment, and rehabilitation evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good moral character and reputation requirement (37 C.F.R. § 11.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: No individual will be registered to practice before the Office unless he or she has established to the satisfaction of the OED Director that he or she possesses good moral character and reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must provide satisfactory proof of possession of good moral character and reputation; the OED Director will not certify registration until, to the Director's satisfaction, the individual demonstrates such character and reputation. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.7(a)(2)(i) and (b)(1)(iii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to answer, fully disclose, and provide supporting documents (37 C.F.R. § 11.7(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: Every individual seeking recognition shall answer all questions in the application and request(s) for comments issued by OED; disclose all relevant facts, dates and information; and provide verified copies of documents relevant to his or her good moral character and reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office guidance: 'You should, therefore, provide the Office of Enrollment and Discipline with all available information, however, unfavorable, even if its relevance is in doubt, with regard to the questions asked below.' Failure to provide requested information can be evidence against the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to update application information promptly (37 C.F.R. § 11.7(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants are responsible for updating all information and answers submitted in or with the application based upon anything occurring between the date the application is signed and the date of registration; updates must be filed within thirty days after the occasion that necessitates the update.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant's failure to timely update answers (e.g., new investigations, disciplinary actions, or admissions of misconduct that arise after signing) is a regulatory violation and may be weighed as lack of candor or responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED investigation upon receipt of adverse information (37 C.F.R. § 11.7(g)(2)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: If OED receives information from any source that reflects adversely on an applicant's good moral character or reputation, the OED Director shall conduct an investigation (typically after the applicant has passed or waived the registration examination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information discovered in such investigations is part of the record the Director may consider in the registration determination; an applicant cannot be certified until the Director is satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof on applicant to demonstrate current good moral character
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual seeking registration bears the burden of establishing to the satisfaction of the OED Director that he or she currently possesses good moral character and reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director requires 'satisfactory proof' and may deny registration where the record (including admissions and investigative findings) shows insufficient evidence of present good moral character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor and truthfulness as paramount considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Candor and truthfulness (to the Office, advisors, and on the application) are central to the moral character determination; candor may be the most important factor for registration before the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: 'No moral character qualification for registration is more important than truthfulness and candor.' The Office relies on applicants' integrity and expects the highest degree of candor and good faith in dealing with the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (Code of Professional Responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered practitioners are prohibited from engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (e.g., 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4) in effect at time of application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissions or proof of such conduct (including fabrication of data, over-reporting sample sizes, etc.) provide strong support for denial of registration; repeated misconduct is especially disqualifying and comparable to grounds used by state bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of pattern, repetition, and duration of misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: A pattern of repeated offenses over an extended period, even if individual acts might be minor, indicates indifference to legal obligation and weighs heavily against a finding of good moral character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer duration and multiple instances of wrongdoing (here, approximately two and one-half years) require a longer and more substantial showing of rehabilitation; case law cited (e.g., Matter of Morgan) supports this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to disclose misconduct (on application or to institutions) is evidence of lack of candor
rubrics_metrics.description: Delays in reporting misconduct to institutional authorities and failure to disclose misconduct on the USPTO application or to update the application until directly questioned constitute an egregious lack of candor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office may treat learning of misconduct via third-party submissions (e.g., Official Gazette comments) as evidence the applicant failed to meet disclosure obligations; initial justifications for negative answers are not dispositive if later admissions show nondisclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of whether misconduct affected patent-related matters
rubrics_metrics.description: If admitted or proven misconduct materially affected work included in patent applications (data, figures, provisional/PCT filings), that fact is of particular concern to the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misconduct tied to materials submitted in patent filings heightens the severity of the misconduct for registration-purpose analysis because practitioners represent applicants before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehabilitation evidence must be meaningful and of sufficient duration (37 C.F.R. § 11.7(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of rehabilitation (community service, counseling, mentoring, letters of support) may be considered but the requirement of proof of rehabilitation is 'firm and fixed' and requires meaningful substance; length of time since misconduct is a key factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short or recent rehabilitative efforts may be insufficient to overcome a recent pattern of misconduct; case law shows that modest rehabilitation over a short period (e.g., two years) can be inadequate to warrant admission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory and statutory authority for standards (35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D) and USPTO regulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress delegated authority to the USPTO Director to govern recognition and conduct of persons before the Office, including requiring demonstration of good moral character and reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory/regulatory authority underpins the Director's ability to promulgate 37 C.F.R. § 11.7 and related procedural requirements; applicants are assessed under those regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office expectation to provide unfavorable information even if relevance is uncertain
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants are instructed to provide OED with all available information, however unfavorable, even if its relevance is in doubt, regarding the questions asked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This admonition supports why omission of potentially relevant facts (even if the applicant believed them not yet 'official') can be disqualifying; applicants should err on the side of disclosure.
